body: This comment is going to focus on my analysis on why this happens. I have another comment coming that will go into my suggested solution. At the bottom of this comment are a number of definitions I have come up with for describing aspects of the TileMapLayer terrain painting system. They're not required reading, and are mostly provided for reference. --- ## Why does this happen? Well, let's walk thru the logic of the algorithm. This can all be quite complex, and it may be important for people to have an understanding if there is discussion. First the targetted constraints are constructed. These are the center bits for each cell in the rectangle, as well as the sides and corners between them and the previously drawn rectangle. The terrain of these constraints matches the painted terrain, and the priority is 10. Then the untargetted constraints are collated. The terrain of these bits match the bits, and the priority is 1. Then, Godot tries to find the best pattern for each cell. In this case, this happens in the following order: For the first cell, these are the scores of each tile in the tile set. A red dot indicates that it failed to meet a targetted constraint, so the score is +10. A green dot indicates that it failed to meet an untargetted constraint, so the score is +1. [Edit: I missed some dots.] The tile that is completely surrounded is chosen because it has the lowest score of 1. Then, the pattern constraints are determined and recorded. These will all have a priority of 5. For the second cell, these are the scores of each tile in the tile set. The new pink dots here indicate pattern constraints, so the score is +5. [Edit: I missed some dots.] Again, the tile that is completely surrounded is chosen, because it has the lowest score of 2. The expected tile (right edge) has a score of 5. And the pattern constraints recorded are as follows. Skipping forward to the fourth cell, these are the scores of each tile in the tile set. The top edge tile is chosen this time, because it has the lowest score of 1. The expected tile (top right corner) has a score of 5. The fifth cell scores very similarly to the first one, except that many tiles are now receiving a lower score due to the pattern constraints. And so on --- ## Definitions (Feel free to skip this) I use "connecting bit" to refer to the parts of the tile map that, on a conceptual level, are shared between cells. It is the corner or side of any given cell. They have a location and an orientation. The bottom connecting bit of one cell and the top connecting bit of its bottom neighbour are the same connecting bit. I use "targetted constraints" to refer to the constraints being applied based on the desired change. As an example, when I fill a cell using connect mode this creates constraints for that cell's center bit, as well as for the bits connecting that cell and whichever neighbours have the same terrain in their center bit. These are "targetted" as they are the constraints being created and used to bring about the desired change. I use "unconstrained bits" to refer to any center or connecting bit that has no constraint applied to it. When Godot determines which pattern best fits each cell, it will ignore patterns with bits that are different to the cell's current pattern if those bits are unconstrained. In essence: unconstrained bits are fixed. I use "untargetted constraints" to refer to those collated immediately after the targetted constraints are constructed. All connecting and center bits of cells that are being painted to will have any center or connecting bit given an untargetted constraint if they do not already have a targetted constraint. This allows these bits to change (as they are no longer unconstrained) so that the best matching pattern can make use of all bits. I use "pattern constraints" to refer to those added while pattern fitting. After Godot determines the best fitting pattern for a cell the bits of that pattern are applied as constraints. This helps ensure consistency across all cells being added in the same operation where the actual available patterns cannot perfectly satisfy the constraints. For determining the best fitting pattern for a cell, Godot calculates a "score" for each possible pattern. A pattern's score is equal to the sum of the "priority" of each constraint that it did *not* satisfy. The pattern with the lowest score is chosen as the best one.

# So what's causing it?

This bug is caused by several factors.

The first is that this isn't a very realistic scenario. The specific setup I have here is designed to highlight the behaviour, and it is unlikely that such a heavily restricted tile set would actually be used like this in a real project. The bug only happens with this setup because I am using "Match Corners and Sides" with such a limited range of patterns. That said, I believe this scenario does a good job of distilling the unexpected behaviour down to a situation that is easy to understand. In more realistic and complex setups it can be difficult to isolate and diagnose this behaviour, and challenging to even know whether what happened is a bug or just a weird edge case.

I hope that, in considering the other 2 factors outlined below, it is apparent that this behaviour is indeed an unintended bug.

The second factor causing this behaviour is that untargetted constraints never have their priority explicitly set (so they use the default priority of 1). The lowest other possible priority is 5, so this means that where all else is equal Godot will prioritise a pattern that matches constraints on a *single* bit over another pattern that matches *at least 4* if those 4 bits are untargetted and that 1 bit is not. (That 1 bit doesn't even have to be a targetted constraint!)

The last factor is caused by how pattern constraints are applied. Pattern constraints will always over-write any existing constraint, and they will do so at a new priority of 5. This results in unexpected behaviour where Godot will effectively ignore constraints that were targetted simply because of the order in which patterns were decided. This creates unexpected and often asymmetrical behaviour.

---

## How to fix?

I imagine this one will require some discussion.

First, I believe that pattern constraints shouldn't be applied if the existing constraint already uses the same terrain (or at the very least, they shouldn't be *lowering* the priority). Pattern constraints exist so that the result can be internally consistent, but because they always over-write whatever constraints already exist, it means that they do a lot more than is intended.

Second is to actually set untargetted constraint priorities, rather than using the default value of 1. By leaving them with a priority of 1, it means that they are almost completely ignored, so neighbouring cells that aren't being painted to are very likely to be updated. Whether this is entirely unintentional or expected is hard to say.

I would suggest setting untargetted constraints to somewhere between 6 and 11. They should be at least as significant as the pattern constraints, and then it's a question of how many untargetted constraints would overcome how many targetted constraints. Assuming the changes to pattern constraints, then...

| Untargetted Priority | # to beat 1 targetted | # to beat 2 targetted | # to beat 3 targetted
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | N/A | N/A | N/A |
| 6 | 2 | 4 | 6 (matches on 5) |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 5 |
| 8-9 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
| 11 | 1 | 2 | 3 |
@groud I think it may be important to hear what of this behaviour is intentional, as well as your thoughts and input on different priority numbers.
